issues.locator: Published §3.3 p.621; same formula in arXiv v2
issues.printed: disc(q)+disc(g)=disc(f)
issues.correction: For local different/discriminant exponents at algebraically closed residue points, use disc(f)=disc(q)+e(q)disc(g), hence μf−aG(1)=e(q)disc(g). The consequence when g is étale is unchanged.
issues.reason: In characteristic 5 take q:x↦u=x² with G=C2, g:u↦t=u³, f:x↦t=x6. The local different exponents are 1,2,5, and aG(1)=1. Thus 1+2≠5 and μf−aG(1)=4≠2, while 1+2·2=5. All maps are separable and f is smooth off 0. The different tower formula multiplies the pulled-back lower different by e(q).

issues.locator: Published Theorem 1.6 proof p.613, fixed-scheme base-change chain; page image checked
issues.printed: (Xi)^σ≅(Xi)^σ×Si{si}
issues.correction: Remove the identification with the closed fiber. Preserve length by étale/strict-henselian base change of the finite-length local fixed algebra with unchanged residue field.
issues.reason: Over algebraically closed k of characteristic 2, X=Spec k[t,z]/(z²+t²z−t), σ(z)=z+t² and σ(t)=t. The map to A¹t is finite flat, X is smooth because ∂F/∂t=1, f is étale off t=0 since ∂F/∂z=t², and σ is an involution. The fixed scheme is k[t,z]/(t²,z²−t)≅k[z]/z4, length 4, supported at the origin. Its closed fiber is k[z]/z², length 2. Thus set-theoretic support at the point does not justify the displayed isomorphism. The needed length-invariance statement survives the proposed henselian repair.

issues.locator: Proof of Proposition 2.7, arXiv v1 p. 5
issues.printed: The source introduces a cover π: C̃ → C_{r²a^{ℓ−1}b²} whose formula on the affine chart z = 1 is π(x, y) = (axy^{−1}, a^{(ℓ−1)/2}(y^{−ℓ} − rb)).
issues.reason: On C̃: ax^ℓ + 2rby^ℓ = 1, with X = axy^{−1} and Y = a^{(ℓ−1)/2}(y^{−ℓ} − rb), one gets Y² − X^ℓ − r²a^{ℓ−1}b² = a^{ℓ−1}(y^{−ℓ} − 1)(y^{−ℓ} − 2rb) (symbolic check for ℓ = 3, 5, 7). This vanishes only where y^ℓ = 1 or 2rby^ℓ = 1, so the map does not land in the curve. With X = axy^{−2}, the difference is identically 0. The point P = π(1, 1) = (a, a^{(ℓ−1)/2}(1 − rb)), which is all the proof uses, is the same for both formulas and lies on the curve because a = 1 − 2rb.
issues.known: Corrected in the published version, Invent. Math. 243 (2025), p. 1135, which prints π(x, y) = (axy^{−2}, a^{(ℓ−1)/2}(y^{−ℓ} − rb)).

issues.locator: Proof of Proposition 2.5, case 𝔪 ≠ 1, p. 1137 (published version); the same text in arXiv v1 p. 7
issues.printed: The source reduces the check to solvability of t_1x² + 2rγ^{nℓ}t_2y² = t_3z² modulo 𝔪 for some units t_1, t_2, t_3 modulo 𝔪. It permits the choice t_1 = t_3 and infers absence of local obstructions at 2-adic primes 𝔭 | 𝔪.
issues.correction: With t_1 = t_3 there can be an obstruction at a 2-adic 𝔭 | 𝔪, whenever v_𝔭(2rγ^{nℓ}) < v_𝔭(𝔪). The conclusion still holds. Repair: replace r by rδ^ℓ, where δ ∈ 𝒪_F is divisible by 𝔭^{v_𝔭(𝔪)} for each 2-adic 𝔭 | 𝔪 and by no other prime (it exists because the class group is finite). Then C_{q^ℓr²δ^{2ℓ}} ≅ C_{q^ℓr²} (§2: C_n ≅ C_{nλ^{2ℓ}}), so Lemma 2.3 and the sets S′, S, Σ are unchanged. The clause r ∉ 𝔭 still holds at the odd ramified primes, where the smooth-conic argument uses it. Now β = 2rδ^ℓγ^{nℓ} ≡ 0 modulo the 2-adic part of 𝔪, so x = y = z = 1 solves the congruence there with t_1 = t_3. Alternatively, keep r and choose t_1 ≠ t_3.
issues.reason: Take F_0 = ℚ, K_0 = ℚ(i) and ℓ = 3, which does not divide Disc = −4. §4 replaces these by F = ℚ(ζ_3) and K = F(i) = ℚ(ζ_12), and K/F is unramified above 3. The prime (2) is inert in F/ℚ, so F_(2) = ℚ_4 is unramified over ℚ_2 with residue field 𝔽_4. F_(2)(i)/F_(2) has conductor exponent 2, so 𝔪 = (4). Since (2) ramifies in K, (2) ∉ S and γ ∉ (2); and r ∉ (2) by Lemma 2.3. Hence v_2(β) = 1. Suppose t x² + βt_2y² ≡ t z² (mod 4) with x, y, z units. Then (z/x)² ≡ 1 + βt_2y²/(tx²) (mod 4), which is ≡ 1 mod 2 but ≢ 1 mod 4. But a unit w with w² ≡ 1 (mod 2) has w ≡ 1 (mod 2), since squaring is bijective on 𝔽_4, and then w² ≡ 1 (mod 4). This is a contradiction. An exhaustive search over the 12 units of ℤ[ζ_3]/4 confirms it. Inertness of a principal prime (p) in K is detected by χ(p) = (−1)^{(N(p)−1)/2}, where N is the norm to ℚ; this is the Hilbert symbol (p, −1) at (2), trivial on global units. For every unit value of β/2 there is no solution with t_1 = t_3 and χ(t_1) = χ(t_2) = −1. Yet admissible residues exist with t_1 ≠ t_3: for β ≡ 2, u_1 = u_2 = 1 + 2ζ_3 and u_3 = u_1 + βu_2 ≡ 3 + 2ζ_3 (mod 4), with norms 3, 3, 7 ≡ 3 (mod 4).

issues.locator: Proof of Proposition 3.1 (sketch), p. 1136 (published version); arXiv v1 p. 6
issues.printed: The source gives the finite singular-series factor, apart from small primes, as ∏_𝔭 lim_{n→∞} Nm(𝔭)(Nm(𝔭) − 1)^{−3} #{(p_1, p_2) : p_1, p_2, p_1 + βp_2 ∈ (𝒪_F/𝔭^n)^×}.
issues.correction: ∏_𝔭 lim_{n→∞} Nm(𝔭)^{3−2n}(Nm(𝔭) − 1)^{−3} #{(p_1, p_2) ∈ (𝒪_F/𝔭^n)² : p_1, p_2, p_1 + βp_2 ∈ (𝒪_F/𝔭^n)^×}: the count needs the normalization Nm(𝔭^{n−1})^{−2}. For 𝔭 ∤ β the local factor is Nm𝔭(Nm𝔭 − 2)/(Nm𝔭 − 1)² = 1 − (Nm𝔭 − 1)^{−2}.
issues.reason: The condition is a condition modulo 𝔭, so the set counted has Nm(𝔭)^{2(n−1)} times as many elements as its reduction mod 𝔭. For 𝔭 ∤ β with q = Nm𝔭, the reduction has (q − 1)(q − 2) elements. The printed n-th term is therefore q^{2n−1}(q − 2)/(q − 1)², which tends to infinity for every 𝔭 with q ≥ 3, so the product as printed diverges. With the normalization the factors are 1 − (q − 1)^{−2} and the product converges.

issues.locator: End of the proof of Proposition 2.5, p. 1137 (published version), with the statement of Proposition 3.1, p. 1135; arXiv v1 pp. 5–7
issues.printed: The source claims that each of the infinitely many constructed triples (p_1, p_2, p_3) gives an ideal 𝔱_{p_1,p_2,p_3} := (p_1^{(ℓ−1)/2} p_2 p_3^{(ℓ−1)/2}) whose sufficiently large prime factors have multiplicity below ℓ. It claims these ideals have infinite support, since finite support would yield infinitely many solutions of an 𝒮-unit equation for a finite prime set 𝒮, contrary to Siegel–Mahler.
issues.correction: The argument needs infinitely many pairwise non-proportional triples. Proposition 3.1 should say so; its proof gives it, since the circle-method count (or Kai's asymptotic) of triples of height ≤ N is ≫ N^{2d}/(log N)^3 with d = [F : ℚ], against O(N^d) triples proportional to a fixed one. The multiplicity claim should be stated for non-proportional triples.
issues.reason: Suppose ε_1 + βε_2 = ε_3 has a solution in units ε_i ∈ 𝒪_F^×. Then for every I-prime π satisfying the congruences, (ε_1π, ε_2π, ε_3π) is a triple as in Proposition 3.1. For it 𝔱 = (π)^ℓ, up to a power of I, so its large prime factor has multiplicity exactly ℓ, contrary to the first sentence. It also yields the same (a, b) = (ε_1/ε_3, γ^{nℓ}ε_2/ε_3) for every π. Proposition 3.1 as stated ('infinitely many triples (p_1, p_2, p_3) (mod 𝒪_F^×)') does not exclude that all but finitely many of its triples are of this form. The paper does not check whether such unit solutions exist for the chosen β. So the step from Proposition 3.1 to the infinitude of X is incomplete as written, though it is repaired by the count in its proof.

issues.locator: Published §2.2.4, second paragraph, p.13, DOI 10.1007/s10240-017-0096-x; also arXiv:1609.00320v1 §2.2.4, p.12. Both parsed passages compared on 22 September 2026; main-PDF screenshot retrieval failed.
issues.correction: Retain a specified topology, or assume the identity between the two complete normed algebras is continuous in one direction. Then open mapping and the valid fixed-topology uniqueness argument apply. The maximum of two complete norms on the same algebra need not be complete.
issues.reason: Let C=C_p, F=Q_p-bar⊂C. Choose t in C outside F, extend t to a transcendence basis of C/F, and extend the automorphism t↦pt of its rational function field to σ∈Aut(C/F). Set ρ_1(x)=|x| and ρ_2(x)=|σ(x)|. Both are complete multiplicative Q_p-algebra norms, but ρ_2(t)=|p|ρ_1(t)≠ρ_1(t). Choose a_n∈F converging to t for ρ_1. Since σ fixes F, this sequence is Cauchy for max(ρ_1,ρ_2), while its individual limits are t and σ^(-1)(t)=p^(-1)t. Thus the maximum is not complete. The report gives all steps and the auxiliary field-theory inputs. This refutes the isolated stronger assertion and its proof step, not the main ramified theorem; an audit of all downstream uses remains open.

issues.printed: p^{i}x_{i,0}=p^{i}fx_{i,1}=\ldots = f^{i}x_{i,i}\neq 0
issues.correction: p^{i}x_{i,0}=p^{i−1}fx_{i,1}=\ldots = f^{i}x_{i,i}\neq 0
issues.reason: The relations imposed are p x_{i,j} = f x_{i,j+1}. Substituting once gives p^i x_{i,0} = p^{i−1}(p x_{i,0}) = p^{i−1} f x_{i,1}, and each further substitution trades one p for one f, so that the chain is p^i x_{i,0} = p^{i−1}f x_{i,1} = p^{i−2}f^2 x_{i,2} = … = f^i x_{i,i}: the total degree in p and f is i throughout. As printed, the second term has degree i+1 and is in fact equal to f^{i+1}x_{i,i+1} = 0, since x_{i,i+1} = 0, which would contradict the assertion that the chain is non-zero. The next sentence, p^{i+1}x_{i,0} = f^i p x_{i,i} = 0, is correct.

issues.locator: the proof of Proposition 5.3.5 (published: Proposition 5.23), the step asserting topological nilpotence of the divided Frobenius; present in arXiv v4 and in the published version, and corrected by the 2025 erratum
issues.printed: The source claims topological nilpotence of divided Frobenius on its kernel and reduces this to A_crys(R) → W(R), arising from the PD-thickening W(R) → R. It constructs A_crys(R) as the PD-envelope of W(R^♭) for ker(W(R^♭) → R), and says that this kernel is topologically generated by V^m([x]) with x ∈ I := ker(R^♭ → R) and m ≥ 0.
issues.correction: The claim is false. The erratum states: 'The key step in the proof of Proposition 5.23 is to show that for a quasiregular semiperfect ring R, the divided Frobenius φ_1 acts topologically nilpotently on the kernel of the map A_crys(R) → W(R). This is not true.' The counterexample, due to Andrew Senger, is R = F_p[x^{1/p^∞}]/x with the element Σ_{k ∈ Z} p^k [x^{1/p^k}] of A_crys(R), which is fixed by the divided Frobenius and lies in the kernel of A_crys(R) → W(R). The erratum diagnoses the gap: 'While the generators of the kernel of A_crys(R) → W(R) used in the proof do topologically generate the kernel in the p-adic topology of A_crys(R), they fail to do so in the p-adic topology of the kernel itself.' The statement of Proposition 5.23 is unaffected: it was already known by the different proofs of Lau, Displays and formal p-divisible groups, and of Zink, The display of a formal p-divisible group, both cited immediately before it, and the erratum records that 'the arguments of this fallacious proof are not used anywhere else in the paper, so this mistake does not affect any of the results stated in the paper'.
issues.reason: Verified against the erratum itself, which was published for exactly this proposition; the mistake was pointed out to the authors by Akhil Mathew and Andrew Senger. Note that the paper proves a similar topological-nilpotence statement twice more, in Lemma 4.88 (arXiv Lemma 4.9.3) for the kernel of Δ_S → Δ_{S̃} and in Lemma 5.15 (arXiv Lemma 5.2.8) for the Breuil–Kisin prism; neither is retracted, and the erratum's sentence that the fallacious argument is used nowhere else applies to them.

issues.locator: Example 7.3, the two stated ranges in the computation of the cyclic homology of k over W(k); in arXiv v2, the version read (the published version could not be consulted)
issues.printed: Using [antieauperiodic] filtrations, the source claims π_i HC(k/W(k)) ≅ W(k)/p^{s+1} when i = 2s ≥ 0 and 0 otherwise, in the range i ≤ 2p−1. It then concludes, for 0 ≤ i ≤ 2p−2, that π_i HC((W(k),(p)/W(k)) ≅ p^{s+1}W(k) when i = 2s and 0 for odd i.
issues.correction: The two ranges should be i ≤ 2p−4 and 0 ≤ i ≤ 2p−4 (equivalently i ≤ 2p−3, since the odd groups vanish).
issues.reason: Both formulas are read off from the sentence immediately before them, that LΩ_k/LΩ_k^{≥s} ≅ W(k)/p^s for s ≤ p−1, applied with s+1 in place of s: π_{2s}HC(k/W(k)) = LΩ_k/LΩ_k^{≥s+1}. That needs s+1 ≤ p−1, i.e. i = 2s ≤ 2p−4. At the first excluded value, i = 2p−2 and s = p−1, the formula would give W(k)/p^p, but LΩ_k here is the p-completed divided power envelope of (p) ⊆ W(k) — that is, W(k) itself — and its Hodge filtration is the divided power filtration, whose p-th step is generated by γ_p(p) = p^p/p!, of p-adic valuation p − 1 since v_p(p!) = 1. So LΩ_k/LΩ_k^{≥p} = W(k)/p^{p−1} and π_{2p−2}HC(k/W(k)) ≅ W(k)/p^{p−1}, not W(k)/p^p; correspondingly the relative group is p^{p−1}W(k), not p^pW(k). The conclusion of the example is unaffected: it is drawn in the range 1 ≤ i ≤ 2p−5, where the odd degrees used are i = 2s+1 ≤ 2p−5, so s ≤ p−3 and s+1 ≤ p−2, well inside the range where the de Rham formula holds.

issues.locator: Theorem 4.1, p.13 of the author copy (= arXiv 1810.04801v2, p.13); the JAMS typeset version was not collated (publisher PDF not obtainable here, verification gap G1)
issues.correction: Definability holds only after shrinking. For some radius 0 < ρ < 1, the restriction of Φ to (∆*_ρ)^n is R_an,exp-definable, and then for every ρ < 1 by compactness of the remaining annular pieces. The reduction in §4.1 must use charts whose shrunken polydisks still cover the compactification.
issues.reason: Counterexample (n = 1, trivial monodromy). Let f(z) = exp(−(1+z)/(1−z)) on the unit disk, so |f| < 1, and τ = 2i + εf with ε small, so that τ(∆) lies in a disk on which π: H → Γ\H is injective (Γ torsion-free, e.g. Γ(3)). τ is the period map of a polarized weight-one integral VHS. But Φ^{−1}(π(2i + ε/e)) contains the points z_n = 2πin/(2 + 2πin), n ≠ 0, where f = 1/e. These form an infinite discrete set accumulating at 1, which is impossible for a fibre of a definable map. The proof itself allows for this: it says 'after maybe shrinking the polydisk' (p.14), and its Siegel set S_H (y > 1) covers only |q| < e^{−2π}. Theorem 1.3 is unaffected, since §4.1 can use finitely many shrunken charts. Checked numerically: |f(z_n) − 1/e| < 1e−8 for 0 < |n| ≤ 2000. Noted by the extraction (item local-outer-boundary-obstruction).

issues.locator: Proof of Lemma 4.5, p.15 of the author copy (= arXiv v2 p.15); the JAMS typeset version was not collated (publisher PDF not obtainable here, verification gap G1)
issues.printed: The proof substitutes z_1 = mz_2 + c into f to define f_{m,c}, for each positive integer m and each real c. It asserts that f_{m,c} satisfies the lemma’s hypotheses and that induction on n yields f_{m,c} ≪ 1 throughout Σ_{n−1}.
issues.correction: State the lemma, and verify its curve hypothesis, on the wider sectors Σ_n^R = {|x_i| < R, y_1 ≥ ⋯ ≥ y_n > 1} for every R, with constants depending on R. The substitution then maps Σ_{n−1}^{R′} into Σ_n^{mR′+c}, and the induction goes through unchanged. In the application in §4.5, the curve bounds come from Schmid's one-variable Corollary 5.29 and the norm estimates of Theorem 4.8, which hold for real parts in any bounded interval; Theorem 1.5 is already stated on H^n_{R,η} for all R.
issues.reason: Σ_n is defined with 0 < x_i < 1 (Definition 4.4). The proof uses c = 0, 1, …, r_1 and m ≥ 1. For c ≥ 1, x_1 = mx_2 + c > 1, so Σ_n ∩ {z_1 = mz_2 + c} is empty. For c = 0 it is only the strip x_2 < 1/m. So the hypothesis gives no information about f_{m,c} on Σ_{n−1}. The functions extend there (the coefficients in O are periodic in x and f is polynomial in x), but the bound is assumed only on Σ_n. With the R-uniform hypothesis, the finite difference in c isolates the top x_1-degree, the Vandermonde step in m isolates each y-power, and |x_1| < 1 on Σ_n finishes the proof, as printed. Noted by the extraction (verification gap G4); the repair is given by this continuation.

issues.locator: §1, p.4 (arXiv v3)
issues.printed: The source characterizes strong divisibility p² of ∆(f) by either two distinct multiple roots of f modulo p in F̄_p or an F_p-root of multiplicity at least 3. It characterizes weak divisibility by p² | ∆(f) together with exactly one multiple root modulo p, lying in F_p and being a simple double root.
issues.correction: This holds for odd p. For p = 2, 4 always divides Δ(f) strongly when 2 | Δ(f), so W^{(2)}_m is empty for even m.
issues.reason: By Stickelberger's congruence, the discriminant of a monic integer polynomial is ≡ 0 or 1 mod 4, so 2 | Δ(f + 2g) implies 4 | Δ(f + 2g) for every g. For example f = x² + 1 ≡ (x + 1)² mod 2 has a single simple double root, yet Δ(x² + a_1x + a_2) = a_1² − 4a_2 ≡ 0 mod 4 whenever a_1 is even. A brute-force check over all f mod p confirms the criterion for p = 3 (n ≤ 5) and p = 5 (n ≤ 4), and finds failures at p = 2 for every n = 2, …, 5. The proofs only use the implication "two multiple roots or a triple root ⇒ strong", which holds at p = 2 as well (in Proposition 2.2), and the tail estimates concern large primes, so nothing else changes.

issues.locator: Proof of Proposition 4.3, p.22 (arXiv v3)
issues.printed: For even n ≥ 4 and a factorization g(x)ḡ(x) over a quadratic extension, the source claims that the splitting field’s degree is at most 2(n/2)!, yielding an index in S_n of at least n(n−1)/2 for the Galois group.
issues.correction: The splitting field has degree at most 2((n/2)!)², so the index is at least C(n, n/2)/2. That is ≥ n(n − 1)/2 only for n ≥ 8. For n = 6 the index can be 10, but n/[S_n : H] ≤ 3/5 < 1 still gives the stated bound. For n = 4 the index can be 3 (Galois group D_4), and the argument yields O_ε(X^{6+4/3+ε}) = O_ε(X^{22/3+ε}) for these quartics. So Proposition 4.3 is proved for n = 4 only in the weaker form #V_4(Z)^red_X = O_ε(X^{22/3+ε}) = O(X^{n(n+1)/2−8/3+ε}).
issues.reason: Over K = Q(√d) the splitting fields of g and ḡ have degree up to (n/2)! each, and their compositum up to ((n/2)!)². The Galois group of f lies in S_{n/2} ≀ S_2, of order 2((n/2)!)². Example: x⁴ − 2 = (x² − √2)(x² + √2) over Q(√2) has Galois group D_4 of order 8 > 2·2! = 4. With [S_4 : D_4] = 3, Dietmann's bound for |a_4| ≤ X⁴ is X^{4/3+ε} per (a_1, a_2, a_3), against the X^{2/(n−1)} = X^{2/3} the proof claims. Every use of Proposition 4.3 (§§2.4, 3.4, (4)) needs only O(X^{n(n+1)/2−1/5}), which X^{10−8/3+ε} satisfies. No main result is affected.

issues.locator: Lemma 5.1 and proof, p.24 (arXiv v3)
issues.printed: The source claims uniqueness of the rings’ Minkowski-reduced bases forces φ(h_i(θ)) = h*_i(θ*) for every i. Taking i = 1, it deduces φ(θ) = θ* + c with c ∈ Z, then concludes g(x) = g*(x) and declares a contradiction.
issues.correction: A Minkowski-reduced basis is unique at best up to the signs of its vectors: with α_1, …, α_n, every ±α_1, …, ±α_n is also Minkowski-reduced. So φ(h_1(θ)) = ±h*_1(θ*), φ(θ) = ±θ* + c, and the correct conclusion is g*(x) = g(x) or g*(x) = (−1)^ng(−x). Lemma 5.1 holds as stated only for pairs not related by x ↦ −x. In Corollaries 1.3 and 1.4 each field then comes from at most two of the counted polynomials, so the lower bounds are unchanged. Remark 5.6 already counts θ ↦ ±θ + c.
issues.reason: Counterexample: g = x³ − 50x + 7 and g* = x³ − 50x − 7 are distinct, have vanishing x²-coefficients and are strongly quasi-reduced. For both, an exhaustive search gives the Minkowski-reduced basis 1, θ, θ² − 33, unique up to sign, with squared lengths 3, 100, 1667. Yet x ↦ −x is an isomorphism Z[x]/(g) ≅ Z[x]/(g*). If "unique" were meant literally, including signs, no lattice would be strongly quasi-reduced and Lemma 5.3 would fail instead.

issues.locator: Proofs of Lemmas 5.2 and 5.3, p.25 (arXiv v3)
issues.printed: Lemma 5.2 identifies Minkowski reduction of Q with γ belonging to F_SL, and says quasi-reduction amounts to t_i ≤ c t_{i+1}, without restrictions on ν. Lemma 5.3 claims density greater than 1 − ε for monic integer polynomials f with nonzero discriminant that are strongly quasi-reduced.
issues.correction: Lemma 5.2: F_SL is a Siegel set, which contains the Minkowski domain but is not equal to it. The proof needs the converse direction for well-separated tori: if t_{i+1}/t_i ≥ C_n for all i (C_n depending on n), then a basis with these Gram–Schmidt lengths is Minkowski-reduced after a unipotent integral change of basis. This holds because each successive shortest extending vector must then have the form ±b_i + Σ_{j<i}c_jb_j. Since the ratios for g(ρx) grow like ρ, the lemma follows. Lemma 5.3: the proof yields quasi-reduction only. Uniqueness of the reduced basis up to sign must be added. For well-separated tori it fails only on the locus where two candidates ±b_i + Σc_jb_j have equal length, a proper closed semialgebraic subset of V_n(R), whose integer points in ρ·B are o(ρ^{n(n+1)/2}).
issues.reason: As written, the equivalence is false, and "strongly" in Lemma 5.3 is asserted without argument. Both steps are standard, and with them the lemmas and Corollaries 1.3–1.4 stand.

issues.locator: Proposition 3.6 and proof, pp.11–12
issues.printed: Proposition 3.6 asserts det(A^top(A^top)^t) det(B^top(B^top)^t) | Δ in Z[W_0]. The proof claims that (A, B) ∈ W_0(C) satisfying det(B^top(B^top)^t) = 0 must have B^top of deficient rank.
issues.correction: Over C, det(MM^t) = 0 does not imply rank M < g (for M = (1, i), MM^t = 0), so the Nullstellensatz argument fails and the statement is false. What the argument does prove: Δ vanishes on the complex locus where B^top (or A^top) has rank < g. So Δ lies in the ideal generated by the g × g minors of B^top (a prime determinantal ideal), and likewise for A^top. On bounded sets this gives |Δ| ≪ Σ|minors| ≪ det(B^top(B^top)^t)^{1/2}, by Cauchy–Binet, and that suffices for Lemma 6.25 with the exponent doubled.
issues.reason: Counterexample for n = 3 (g = 1): A = [[0, 0, 1], [0, 0, 0], [1, 0, 1]] and B = [[0, 1, 1], [1, 1, 0], [1, 0, 0]] lie in W_0(Z). Then f_{A,B} = −y(x² − 3xy + y²) and Δ = 5, while det(A^top(A^top)^t)det(B^top(B^top)^t) = 1·2 = 2 ∤ 5. At random integral points the claimed divisibility held in only 6 of 37 cases for n = 3 and 0 of 40 for n = 5. Δ vanished at all 12 random points with rank-1 B^top for n = 5.

issues.locator: Lemma 7.2 and proof, pp.52–53; proof of Theorem 3, p.53
issues.printed: Lemma 7.2 claims that isomorphic rank-n rings R_f and R_{f*} imply SL_2(Z)-equivalence of f(x, y) and f*(x, y). The proof invokes unique Minkowski-reduced bases to say that φ sends R_f's basis 1, ζ_1, …, ζ_{n−1} respectively to R_{f*}'s basis 1, ζ*_1, …, ζ*_{n−1}.
issues.correction: Minkowski-reduced bases are unique at best up to the signs of their vectors, so φ(ζ_i) = ±ζ*_i. The conclusion is only that f* is GL_2(Z)-equivalent to f, e.g. f*(x, y) = f(−x, y). In the proof of Theorem 3, choose B so that no two of its elements are GL_2(Z)-equivalent (GL_2(Z) also acts discretely). The bound is unchanged.
issues.reason: Counterexample for n = 3: f = x³ − x²y + xy² + y³, an S_3 cubic (disc −44), is strongly Minkowski-reduced. An exhaustive search gives the reduced basis 1, ζ_1, ζ_2 with unique minima up to sign. f*(x, y) = f(−x, y) = −x³ − x²y − xy² + y³ has the same lattice R_{f*} = R_f, since ζ*_i = ±ζ_i, so it is strongly Minkowski-reduced too. But f* is not SL_2(Z)-equivalent to f. Otherwise f would have a stabilizer element δ of determinant −1, and −δ would be a nontrivial automorphism of R_f in the twisted GL_2(Z)-action, which is impossible for an order in a non-Galois cubic field. Part I's Lemma 5.1 has the same sign gap (its E10).

issues.locator: Lemma 2.56, second assertion, p.101 of the published version; the same wording is arXiv v1 Lemma 2.37 (p.20), v2 Lemma 2.50 (p.26) and v3 Lemma 2.56 (p.29)
issues.printed: The source fixes D and takes a semiample Q-Cartier Q-divisor A with A ∼_Q M + Λ. Here M is effective Cartier and its support contains no exceptional curve of Y → X; −δD ≤ Λ ≤ δD with δ > 0. For x ∈ F ∩ M having multiplicity k ∈ Z_{>0} in M, it claims ε_sa(A; x) tends to k as δ → 0.
issues.correction: Only a lower bound holds. For every rational γ with 0 < γ < k there is δ₀ > 0, depending only on f, D and γ, such that ε_sa(A; x) = ε(A; x) ≥ k − γ for all δ < δ₀ and all such A, M, Λ and x. Equivalently, liminf_{δ→0} ε_sa(A; x) ≥ k, uniformly. This is exactly what the printed proof establishes; there is no upper bound.
issues.reason: Counterexample with Λ = 0. Let k be a field of characteristic p > 0, X = A²_k, and f: Y → X the blow-up of the origin with exceptional curve E = F. Let M be the sum of the strict transforms of the two axes. Then M ∼ −2E, so M is effective, Cartier, globally generated over X (O_Y(−E) = m·O_Y) and has no exceptional component. Let x = E ∩ (strict transform of the y-axis), so mult_x M = 1 = k. Blow up x, with exceptional curve G and strict transform E′. Then E′² = −2, G² = −1, E′·G = 1 and π*M − tG ∼ −2E′ − (2+t)G, which has degree 2 − t on E′ and t on G. Hence ε(M; x) = 2. At t = 2 the ideal (x, y²) pulls back to O(−E′ − 2G) (charts x = ab, y = b, then a = c, b = cd, giving c²d, and a = ef, b = f, giving f²). So π*M − 2G ∼ −2E′ − 4G is globally generated and ε_sa(M; x) = 2. Taking A = M and Λ = 0 (any D), ε_sa(A; x) = 2 for every δ, not converging to k = 1. The proof only shows that π*A − (k − γ)E is nef. The consumers need only the lower bound: Proposition 8.15 (p.173) uses the first assertion ε_sa(M; x) ≥ 1, which is correct, and Claim 8.21 (p.178) needs ε_sa > 2 for k = 3. So the paper's results are unaffected. Checked on the page image and by exact arithmetic. Noted by the extraction (diagnostic A, gap-seshadri-limit); verified and proved in the corrected form by this continuation.

issues.locator: Proposition 6.28, p.154 of the published version (and arXiv v3 Proposition 6.28, p.71)
issues.printed: Proposition 6.28 assumes a Q-divisor Δ ≥ 0 on X with (X, Δ) globally +-regular, or completely purely globally +-regular over R, respectively. If Δ_Y ≥ 0 and K_Y + Δ_Y = f*(K_X + Δ), it claims (Y, Δ_Y) is globally +-regular in both respective cases.
issues.correction: The conclusion in the resp. case is "completely purely globally +-regular over R", with the pure boundary S_Y the strict transform of S and B_Y = Δ_Y − S_Y. This is what arXiv v2 (Proposition 6.28, p.64) prints, and arXiv v1 (Proposition 6.22, p.48) prints "purely ... purely".
issues.reason: The printed resp. conclusion is false. Take R = k[[t]] with k of characteristic p, X = Y = Spec R, f = id and Δ = S = V(t). Then (X, S) is purely globally +-regular. For a finite normal R′ ⊇ R with uniformizer s and ramification e, the map R → s^{1−e}R′ splits because R′ is R-free and 1 ∉ t·s^{1−e}R′ = sR′. But (X, S) is not globally +-regular: already for the identity cover, a splitting of O_X → O_X(S) = t^{−1}R would send 1 = t·t^{−1} into tR. The cited proof (Proposition 6.26, which applies because R is complete, together with Lemma 4.27 with B′ = B_Y) proves the pure conclusion. The consumer in Theorem 7.14 (p.165) uses the pure conclusion. In arXiv v3 the qualifier is visibly garbled as "( ly globally +-regular, resp.)", so the published wording is a typesetting slip. Checked on the page images of v3 p.71 and published p.154. Noted by the extraction (diagnostic B, gap-pure-birational); the version history was established by this continuation.

issues.locator: Theorem 1.19 of the introduction (= Theorem 7.3), and Remark 7.4(2) (arXiv v4, the version read)
issues.printed: The source takes K nonarchimedean, complete, and algebraically closed; a classical affinoid K-algebra A of dimension d; a prime ℓ; and an étale sheaf F on Spec(A) with ℓ-power torsion. Assuming A smooth or ℓ different from K's residue characteristic, it asserts H^i(Spec(A)_ét, F) = 0 for i > d.
issues.correction: The disjunct 'if A is smooth' is not proved in the paper at this generality. Theorem 7.3, which Theorem 1.19 is labelled as, proves the vanishing above degree d only for ℓ prime to the residue characteristic; the smooth case is claimed only in Remark 7.4(2), only for constant coefficients, and only as an adaptation: 'The algebraization method used to prove Lemma 7.8 below can be adapted to prove this statement when A is smooth (in the sense of rigid spaces) and F is constant, thanks to [Elkik, Theorem 7 and Remark 2 on page 587].' Either the introduction should restrict the smooth case to constant coefficients and point at Remark 7.4(2), or the adaptation should be written out for arbitrary ℓ-power torsion sheaves.
issues.reason: Theorem 7.3 as printed has two parts: (1) H^i = 0 for i > d + 1 for every torsion sheaf, and (2) H^i = 0 for i > d when F is ℓ-power torsion with ℓ prime to the residue characteristic. Neither mentions smoothness of A, and Remark 7.4 opens 'We would expect that part (2) of Theorem 7.3 holds for arbitrary torsion sheaves', listing the smooth constant-coefficient case as one of two special cases that are 'within reach'. No proof of the smooth case for non-constant ℓ-power torsion sheaves appears in Section 7, and the reduction of Theorem 7.3 to constant coefficients runs through Proposition 7.9 for the two cases actually stated there, not for the smooth case.

issues.locator: Proposition 51 and Theorem 9, Appendix A, pp.36–37 (published version)
issues.printed: "Proposition 51. Suppose L is defined over a number field. Then inf_{φ ∈ Aut(ℙ¹)} ‖a₀(φ*L)‖ = e^{−poly_n(δ_L)}. Proof. … Now the operator L′ := L + 1 is also Fuchsian …"
issues.correction: Assume in addition that L + 1 is Fuchsian. This holds when every finite zero of a₀ has order ≤ n and deg a₀ ≥ n, and in particular for the Legendre Picard–Fuchs operator (87), a₀ = λ(1−λ), n = 2, which is the only operator to which the paper applies Theorem 9. Under this normalization the proof of Proposition 51 is correct, and Theorem 9 follows as written.
issues.reason: For a general Fuchsian operator, L + 1 need not be Fuchsian, and both statements fail. Take L = ∂_t, which is Fuchsian: its only singular point ∞ is regular singular (∂_t = −z(z∂_z), z = 1/t). Then φ(s) = κs gives φ*L = κ^{-1}∂_s and inf_φ ‖a₀(φ*L)‖ = 0. In Theorem 9 take b(t) = (t − t₀)/(2r) (|b| ≤ 1 on D^{1/2}) and f = (t − t₀)²/(4r), so j_z f(t₀) = 0 while |∂_z f(t₀ + r/2)| = r/4, unbounded in r. Here L + 1 = ∂ + 1 has an irregular singularity at ∞. Theorems 1–8 are unaffected.

issues.locator: Lemma 4.5.11, second line, p.663 (published version; the same in arXiv v3–v4)
issues.printed: The source states dim H¹(Γ(5), F₃)^{SL₂(F₅)} = 0 and asserts that, for N = 3, 4, 5, the result persists when these modules are replaced by their semisimplifications.
issues.correction: dim H¹(Γ(5), 𝔽₅)^{SL₂(𝔽₅)} = 0 (coefficients 𝔽₅), and likewise for its semisimplification.
issues.reason: Diagram (4.5.10) requires ℓ | N, and the proof of Theorem 4.5.2 takes N = ℓ ∈ {3, 5}, so ℓ = 5 is the case used. As printed the statement is false: SL₂(𝔽₅) is perfect, so inflation–restriction for Γ(5) ⊴ SL₂(ℤ) makes restriction H¹(SL₂(ℤ), 𝔽₃) = Hom(ℤ/12, 𝔽₃) ≅ 𝔽₃ → H¹(Γ(5), 𝔽₃)^{SL₂(𝔽₅)} injective (the character SL₂(ℤ) → SL₂(𝔽₃) → ℤ/3 stays nontrivial on Γ(5), which maps onto SL₂(𝔽₃)). Over 𝔽₃ the semisimplification claim also fails: H¹(Γ(5), ℚ) = 3 + 3′ + 5 as an A₅-module, and the 5-dimensional character, with Brauer character (5, 1, 0, 0) on the 3-regular classes, reduces mod 3 to 1 + 4. Over 𝔽₅ the lemma holds: H¹(SL₂(ℤ), 𝔽₅) = 0 and H²(SL₂(𝔽₅), 𝔽₅) = 0 (Lemma 4.5.5) give vanishing invariants, and 3, 3′, 5 reduce to the Brauer irreducibles 3, 3, 5 of PSL₂(𝔽₅), none trivial.

issues.locator: §4.4, the sentence before Lemma 4.4.4, p.659, and its use in (4.4.9)–(4.4.10), p.660 (published version; the same since arXiv v3)
issues.printed: The source asserts that π : ⟨E, Γ(N)⟩ ∩ Γ0(p) → B is a natural surjective map and identifies Γ(Np) as its kernel.
issues.correction: For N > 2 the kernel of reduction mod p on ⟨E, Γ(N)⟩ ∩ Γ₀(p) is ⟨E, Γ(N)⟩ ∩ Γ(p), which contains Γ(Np) with index 2. Restrict to Γ(N) ∩ Γ₀(p), where the kernel is Γ(Np): Lemma 4.4.4 holds there, and it gives ⟨G ∩ Γ(Np), A⁻¹GA ∩ Γ₀(p) ∩ Γ(N)⟩ = Γ(N) ∩ Γ₀(p); adjoining E gives (4.4.9) as printed. Twisting π by the sign x ≡ ±I mod N works equally.
issues.reason: Some x ∈ SL₂(ℤ) has x ≡ −I mod N and x ≡ I mod p (SL₂(ℤ) → SL₂(ℤ/Np) is onto). It lies in ⟨E, Γ(N)⟩ ∩ Γ₀(p) and in ker π, but not in Γ(Np). So, as written, ker(f₁, π) = G ∩ Γ(p), and the deduction yields (4.4.9) only with G ∩ Γ(p). That is weaker than the (4.4.10) used in the proof of Theorem 4.3.1, where f(pτ) is known to be invariant only under G ∩ Γ(2Np). The proof of Lemma 4.4.4 already works on Γ(N) ∩ Γ₀(p): (f₁, f₂) stays surjective there, and π(γ) still generates the unipotent radical. So the corrected deduction goes through, and Theorems 4.3.1–4.3.2 stand.

issues.locator: Proof of Theorem 7.1, p.41 (choice of η_v at finite places) (arXiv v2; published Annals version not collated)
issues.printed: For every non-archimedean place v of K, the source chooses η_v := min{1, |t₁(t₁ − 1)|_v, |t₂(t₂ − 1)|_v}. It asserts (µ_{t_i,v}, m_{F,η,v})_v = (µ_{t_i,v}, [F]_v)_v because the potentials of µ_{t_i,v} are constant on radius-η_v disks.
issues.correction: At places v | 2 take η_v := |2|_v · min{1, |t₁(t₁ − 1)|_v, |t₂(t₂ − 1)|_v}. The claim is then true: in the potentially good range the support of µ_{t,v} is a type II point of diameter |Δ_t|_v^{1/6} = |2|_v^{2/3}|t(t − 1)|_v^{1/3} ≥ |2|_v min{1, |t(t − 1)|_v}, and in the bad-reduction ranges of Proposition 3.5 smaller radii are harmless. (7.5) grows by Σ_{v|2} r_v log 2 = log 2, which is divided by 2|F| and absorbed into C(ε).
issues.reason: The claim fails at v | 2 when |t_i(t_i − 1)|_v = 1. There η_v = 1, but µ_{t_i,v} is a point mass at ζ_{a,R} with R < 1. Indeed λ_{t,v}(0) = λ_{t,v}(ζ_{0,1}) = 0 and f_t(ζ_{0,1}) = ζ_{0,1/|4|}, so the support lies in a residue class of ζ_{0,1} other than that of 0. For x ∈ D(a,R), λ(ζ_{x,1}) − λ(x) = log(1/R) > 0, so the non-archimedean term of Proposition 7.3 is positive, not 0. Counterexample: take ω a primitive cube root of 1 and t₁ ≠ t₂ the roots of t² − (6ω² − 4)t − (3ω − 4) = 0 (discriminant 48ω(1 − ω) ≠ 0). Then ψ₃(ω, t_i) = 0, so x = ω ∈ π(E_{t₁}[3]) ∩ π(E_{t₂}[3]) ⊆ F. Also t₁t₂ = 4 − 3ω and (t₁ − 1)(t₂ − 1) = 15 + 3ω are 2-adic units, so |t_i(t_i − 1)|_v = 1 and η_v = 1. The reduction is supersingular (|j(t_i)|_v ≤ |2|^8), so the 3-torsion reduces to non-identity points and x ∈ D(a_i, R_i). The bound therefore acquires a positive term that is not divided by |F|, which would break the small-height case of Theorem 8.1. With the corrected η_v the equality holds and all later statements stand.

issues.locator: Proof of Theorem 1.4, p.36 (arXiv v3; published Annals version not collated)
issues.printed: The source invokes Northcott and Torelli to claim that only finitely many curves C_Q̄, up to Q̄-isomorphism, satisfy h(ι([Jac(C_Q̄)])) < c1. It says Theorem 1.4 follows by using Raynaud’s Manin–Mumford result individually for these curves.
issues.correction: For each of the finitely many curves C a bound for #((C − P₀) ∩ Jac(C)_tors) uniform in P₀ ∈ C(ℚ̄) is needed, because Theorem 1.4 quantifies over all P₀. For g ≥ 3 it follows from Raynaud's theorem for the surface C − C ⊆ Jac(C): its torsion lies in finitely many points and elliptic torsion cosets, and a coset t + E pulls back to a curve in C × C with no component C × {P₀}, so each P₀ meets it in boundedly many points. For g = 2, C − C = Jac(C), and a uniform Manin–Mumford for the translates C − P₀ is required, e.g. Kühne's later uniform Manin–Mumford theorem (arXiv:2101.10272), which proves Theorem 1.4 without the dependence on d.
issues.reason: Raynaud's theorem gives, for each embedding C − P₀ ⊆ Jac(C), a finite set, with no control of its size as P₀ varies over the infinitely many points of C(ℚ̄). The statement is true, but the displayed step does not prove it.

issues.correction: No bound ℓ_A ≪ log ε_D holds uniformly. ℓ_A can be about √D while log ε_D is about log D. Eichler's argument bounds the word length of the geometric code of the closed geodesic, which is a different quantity from ℓ_A.
issues.reason: Take a odd with a² + 4 squarefree, for example a = 13 or 101 (D = 173 or 10205 = 5·13·157). Then D = a² + 4 ≡ 5 (mod 8) is a fundamental discriminant, and a² + 4 is squarefree for a positive proportion of a. For the principal class, (a + √D)/2 has regular continued fraction [a; a, a, …]. A regular partial quotient a in an odd position becomes a run of a − 1 twos in the minus continued fraction, so the reduced period is ((a + 2, 2, …, 2)) with a − 1 twos, and ℓ_A = a. Meanwhile ε_D = ((a + √D)/2)² = (a² + 2 + a√D)/2, so log ε_D ≈ 2 log a, and ℓ_A / log ε_D → ∞. A direct computation for a = 5, 7, 13, 21, 51, 101, 201, 401 gives ℓ_A = a. In each case the product of the reduced w over the period equals ε_D, as in (6.3), which confirms that ℓ_A is the paper's quantity. The remark is not used elsewhere in the paper.
issues.known: Partly: P. Humphries and A. C. Nordentoft, "Sparse equidistribution of geometric invariants of real quadratic fields", arXiv 2211.05890v2 (28 August 2025), Remark 3.22, observe that Eichler's argument bounds the geometric code of the geodesic and not ℓ_A (the arithmetic code), so the remark is unsupported. issues.reason: The forms φ are normalized by a(1) = 1 in (5.7), p.962, and the Shimura relation in Theorem 4 forces this too. [12, Theorem 5] (Duke 1988, p.85, read on the page image) bounds the coefficients of a spectral weight-1/2 form with eigenvalue 1/4 + t² by |λ|^A ch(πt/2)|n|^{−2/7+ε}. Here t = r/2, so Theorem 4 gives |Weyl(⟨φ, φ⟩^{−1}φ, χ)| ≪ r^C cosh²(πr/4)|D|^{3/4−2/7+ε}. That bound has an exponential factor, which (6.6) omits. The factor cannot simply be dropped. For a(1) = 1, Rankin–Selberg unfolding gives ⟨φ, φ⟩ ≍ L(1, sym²φ)/cosh(πr), so ⟨φ, φ⟩^{−1}φ is about e^{πr/2} times the unit vector u. As printed, (6.6) would therefore make the Weyl integrals of u exponentially small in r, which the cited results do not give. For u the two exponentials cancel: Weyl(u, χ) = ‖φ‖ Weyl(⟨φ, φ⟩^{−1}φ, χ) ≪ L(1, sym²φ)^{1/2} r^C |D|^{13/28+ε}, and L(1, sym²φ) ≪ r^ε. The coefficient bound "c(φ) ≪ |r|^{−A}" used for Theorem 2 on p.969 holds for u, so Theorem 2 stands. Noted by the extraction ("The spectral norm gate").

issues.locator: Published Theorem 2.17 pp.117–119, especially p.119 root descent; author version pp.13–14
issues.correction: For arbitrary, possibly nonreduced S, require the rank-r reduced characteristic invariant computed by local Morita reduction to equal a; prove its independence and descent. The weaker conditions of support on Z'_a and characteristic polynomial a^(p^d) do not recover a. Restricting S to reduced schemes repairs Frobenius injectivity but is insufficient for the later infinitesimal argument.
issues.reason: Let R=k[ε]/ε² in characteristic p≥5 and Z an elliptic curve with nonzero differential ω. In the trace-free rank-three Hitchin base take a(λ)=λ³+εω²λ. It differs from a₀=λ³, but a^p=a₀^p and a(0)=0. The 𝒟-module attached to the rank-three canonical zero-p-curvature connection is supported on the zero section, hence on Z'_a; its pushforward has rank 3p and polynomial λ^(3p)=a^p. It satisfies the printed right-hand conditions but reconstructs the zero-invariant connection, not one with invariant a. Thus the canonical BNR essential-image characterization is insufficient, as well as the stated root-uniqueness inference. This does not provide a counterexample to Theorems 1.4 or 1.6.

issues.locator: Proposition 21, Proposition 30 and Theorem 3, pp.3, 21, 32–33 (arXiv v3)
issues.printed: Proposition 21 claims that every unexceptional z ∈ M − K has a positive c⋆ with M(z, a) = e^{βa}(c⋆(z) + o(1)) as a → ∞. Proposition 30 claims, for fixed λ and z⁽⁰⁾, a constant c⋆(λz⁽⁰⁾) satisfying a_L(λz⁽⁰⁾) = … = c⋆(λz⁽⁰⁾) + o(1). The source says Proposition 30 combined with Lemma 29 establishes Proposition 21.
issues.correction: Add an argument for c⋆ > 0. Fix a small ε₀ > 0 and a point z of the orbit with α(z) > max(C₁, 2C₂^{1/2}ε₀^{−1/2}). Iterating Lemma 26 with ε₀ as in the proof of (3.25) gives log log(λz)_n ≥ log(γ(λ).f(z))_n − 2ε₀ for all λ ∈ Λ′. So M(z, a) ≥ N(f(z), a − 2ε₀) ≥ ½ min_∆ h · e^{β(a−2ε₀)} for large a, since h > 0 is continuous on the compact ∆ (Theorems 13 and 37). Hence c⋆(z) > 0, and then c > 0 in Theorem 3.
issues.reason: Proposition 30 only proves that a_L converges and that its limits are bounded. Neither Lemma 29 nor Proposition 30 bounds c⋆ below. Baragar's estimate (log R)^{β+o(1)} does not exclude c = 0 either, since it allows, say, (log R)^β/log log R. Theorem 3 asserts c > 0, and the constant is Σ over base points of (log z_n⁽⁰⁾)^β c_∞(z⁽⁰⁾), so positivity needs this missing step. The step is routine with the paper's own lemmas.

issues.locator: §9, p. 30 (arXiv v1); checked on the page image
issues.printed: The source describes an apparent D_3 system but claims that the Weyl-invariant quadratic form q(s_1, s_2, s_3) = s_1² + s_2² + s_3³ − ¼(s_1 + s_2 + s_3)², in place of the ordinary dot product, realizes C_3. It lists the simple roots as α_1 = (0, 1, −1), α_2 = (1, −1, 0), α_3 = (0, 2, 2).
issues.correction: On the space of characters (s_1, s_2, s_3), where the paper has just written the Weyl action, the invariant form is s_1² + s_2² + s_3² + (s_1 + s_2 + s_3)², and the simple roots are (0, 1, −1), (1, −1, 0), (−1, 1, 1), of type C_3. The printed form, with s_3² for the misprinted s_3³, is the invariant form on the dual space of cocharacters (u_1, u_2, u_3). There the vectors (0, 1, −1), (1, −1, 0), (0, 2, 2) are the images 2α^∨/q(α^∨) of the simple roots, and α_3^∨ = (0, 1, 1).
issues.reason: The paper's reflection for α_3 is r_3(s) = (s_1 + s_2 + s_3, −s_3, −s_2), which is s − ⟨s, α_3^∨⟩α_3 with α_3^∨ = (0, 1, 1) and α_3 = (−1, 1, 1). The computation gives q(r_3 s) − q(s) = (5/4)((s_1 + s_2 + s_3)² − s_1²) ≠ 0, so q is not invariant on characters. A form a|s|² + b(Σs)² is invariant under r_1, r_2, r_3 exactly when a = b. Its inverse matrix I − J/4 gives the printed q on cocharacters. With the roots (0, 1, −1), (1, −1, 0), (−1, 1, 1) and the printed coroots, the Cartan matrix is [[2, −1, 0], [−1, 2, −1], [0, −2, 2]], of type C_3. All this was checked by computation in exact arithmetic. The positive chamber stated next, Re s_1 > Re s_2 > |Re s_3|, is correct, and nothing later uses q.

For p = 3, use (3,0,0) when k ≡ 9 mod 27; when k ≡ 18 mod 27, use (3y, 3, 0) with y² = (k − 9)/9 ≡ 1 mod 3; when 27 | k, use (3, 3, x₃) with x₃ a root of x₃² − 9x₃ + 18 − k, whose discriminant 9 + 4k = 9(1 + 4k/9) is a 3-adic square. Each is an exact ℤ_p-point, since the required square roots exist in ℤ₂, resp. ℤ₃.

issues.locator: Proposition B.12, p.50 (arXiv v3)
issues.correction: Only the qualitative statement is right: δ₂(k) = 0 iff k ≡ 3 (mod 4), and otherwise δ₂(k) ≥ 3/4. In (1), δ₂(k) = (3/8)(1 + χ₄(k))(2 − χ₈(k)), i.e. 3/4 for k ≡ 1 (mod 8) and 9/4 for k ≡ 5 (mod 8); (2) and (3)(a), (c), (e) are consistent with direct counts. (3)(b) and (4)(b) involve 2^{−(η−6)/2} with η odd, which is irrational. (3)(d) fails: δ₂ = 7/4 for 4 − k = 16w with w ≡ 1, 3, 5 mod 8 and 11/4 for w ≡ 7. In (4), (c) holds only for w ≡ 1 (mod 4) (δ₂ = 1 when w ≡ 3 mod 4), and (a), (d), (e) fail in every class tested: for example δ₂ = 11/8 at η = 4, 5 with w ≡ 1 (mod 4), and δ₂(k) → 1 as η → ∞ (35/32 at η = 8), whereas the printed values tend to 5/2. ((3)(e) is read with (−1)^w = −1 for odd w.) The formulas must be re-derived from Lemmas B.9–B.10.
issues.reason: Brute-force counts modulo 2⁶, 2⁷ and 2⁸ give δ₂(1) = 3/4, δ₂(5) = 9/4, δ₂(16) = 11/8 and δ₂(24) = 1, against the printed 3/2, 9/2, 5/4 and 5/2. issues.correction: Retain the underlying-space quotient theorem. Replace the component formula with separate valid restricted theorems for the locally spatial period torsors, compact level quotients and compact Galois descent actually used. A compact-only replacement is insufficient for Proposition3.12.
issues.reason: Let C be an algebraically closed characteristic-p perfectoid field, F=underline Zp times Spa(C,OC), and let the DISCRETE locally profinite group Z act by translations. Scholze11.12 realizes F as a perfectoid space; the free pro-etale relation coproduct_Z F defines a quotient diamond G and a Z-torsor. Scholze12.7–12.9 give |G|=Zp/Z with quotient topology. Every integer orbit is dense. Any nonempty saturated open has closed invariant complement, which would contain a dense orbit if nonempty; hence the quotient is indiscrete. It has more than one point (Zp is uncountable, Z countable), so it is connected, whereas pi0(F)/Z=Zp/Z has many elements. Proposition3.12 and6.6(2) use this false generality. This disproves the lemma, not by itself the geometric main theorems.

issues.locator: Proof of Theorem 5.6, p. 25 (arXiv v3; the same text in v1 and v2)
issues.printed: The proof asserts that in Ā, the ideal generated by the expression (f′_{j+1}) + (f′_{j+1}, …, f′_h)² has the radical of IĀ. It then invokes prime avoidance to choose f″ in (f′_{j+1}, …, f′_h)² for which f′_{j+1} + f″ is a nonzerodivisor in Ā.
issues.correction: Replace the upper index h (= height I) by m (the number of minimal generators): take f″ ∈ (f′_{j+2}, …, f′_m)² ⊆ I². By Nakayama IĀ = (f′_{j+1}, …, f′_m)Ā, so (f′_{j+1}) + (f′_{j+2}, …, f′_m)² has the radical of IĀ, which lies in no associated prime of Ā because IĀ contains a non-zero-divisor; Kaplansky's Theorem 124 then gives f″. Since f″ ∈ I² ⊆ (t)², the new generators keep the form (5.4) and minimality. Theorem 5.6 is true.
issues.reason: When h < m the first h minimal generators need not generate I up to radical. Example: P = O[[t1,t2]], I = (t1(ϖ+t2), ϖt2(ϖ+t2), t1t2), a minimal generating set of the form (5.4) with d = (1, 2, ∞). A = P/I is in C_O(0) (I·P_{(t)} = (t1,t2)), the minimal primes of I are (t1,ϖ), (t1,t2), (t1,ϖ+t2), (ϖ,t2), so h = 2 = n − c and dim A = 1 = c + 1, while m = 3. For j = 1, f1 = t1(ϖ+t2) and Ā = P/(f1) has associated primes (t1) and (ϖ+t2). The printed ideal is (f′_2) and every element of f′_2 + (f′_2)² lies in (ϖ+t2), so it is a zero-divisor: the step fails. With the correction, f2 = f′_2 + (t1t2)² is a non-zero-divisor on Ā.

Its H_0-part is the displayed quotient, but the higher Koszul homology is also there. The missing classes are O-torsion, so the conclusions that follow — Ext^c_A(O,O) ≅ O·η_{m+1}⋯η_n ⊕ (torsion) and F^c_A(O) generated by the class of η_{m+1}⋯η_n — are correct.

issues.printed: The theorem asserts δ_A(M) ≥ δ_B(M), and characterizes equality by length_O Φ_A = length_O Φ_B.
issues.correction: With r := rank_{B_{p_B}}(M_{p_B}) (= rank_{A_{p_A}}(M_{p_A}), since A_{p_A} ≅ B_{p_B}), δ_A(M) − δ_B(M) = r·(length_O Φ_A − length_O Φ_B) ≥ 0. So δ_A(M) ≥ δ_B(M), and when r ≠ 0 equality holds if and only if length_O Φ_A = length_O Φ_B; when r = 0 equality always holds. (r ≠ 0 holds, for example, when M is supported at p_B with grade(p_B, M) ≥ c, since M is then free at p_B.)

issues.locator: Definition of C_O, §2 'Wiles defect', p. 16; used in §4 'Dualizing complexes', p. 21, 5.1, p. 24, §6, and §9 'Complete intersection rings', p. 40
issues.printed: At p. 16, the source defines C_O via pairs (A, λ_A): A is local, complete and noetherian; λ_A : A → O is local and surjective; and A is regular at p_A := Ker(λ_A). At p. 21 it claims that every A belonging to C_O arises as a quotient of a regular ring, specifically a power series ring over O, and therefore possesses a dualizing complex. At p. 40 it writes every local A in C_O as P/I with P := O[[t]].
issues.correction: Require A to be an O-algebra, λ_A a map of O-algebras and morphisms O-algebra maps, as the Introduction (p. 4, 'A a complete local noetherian O-algebra') and the Glossary (p. 80, 'a surjective map in CNL_O') say. Then every A in C_O is O[[t]]/I with I ⊆ (ϖ)(t) + (t)², and §§5–9 apply as written. (Existence of a dualizing complex holds in general by Cohen's structure theorem.)

issues.locator: Proof of Theorem 10.6(1), pp. 46–47
issues.printed: The proof defines R′ as R∞'s image in End_{S∞}(P(C)), asserts dim R′ = dim R∞ because P(C) is maximal Cohen–Macaulay over R∞, and says R′ is finite over S∞. Adapting [8, Lemmas 3.6 and 3.7] is said to yield a lift S∞ → R∞ of S∞ → R′ making R∞ finite over S∞.
issues.correction: Choose ϕ∞ independently of 𝔆: lift S∞ → Q̄ := lim_{s,a} R(s, a, ∞), which is finite over S∞ (Q̄/(n, ϖ) ≅ R_0/ϖ). Then modify the lifts of y, w by elements of K = Ker(R∞ → Q̄) one at a time so that, with ϖ, they cut out a finite-length quotient of R∞ (prime avoidance on R∞/(ϖ, earlier lifts), using dim R∞/ϖ = dim S∞/ϖ − ℓ_0 and dim Q̄ = dim R∞). The theorem's claim is true, but the printed step does not prove it.
issues.reason: [8, Lemma 3.6] (arXiv:2108.09729v2, p. 11) assumes (P): S ↪ R making R finite free, and (CI): R̃ a complete intersection, O-flat and equidimensional; neither holds for S∞ → R∞ here (dim R∞ = dim S∞ − ℓ_0 < dim S∞ when ℓ_0 > 0, and R∞ need not be Cohen–Macaulay), so the lemma does not apply as stated. The proof also takes R′ from an unspecified 𝔆, although ϕ∞ must serve the whole functor P, and dim R′ = dim R∞ needs P(𝔆) ≠ 0. Finiteness of R∞ over S∞ is not used later in an essential way (Theorem 11.3 can pass through R′).

issues.locator: Remark 12.2, second paragraph, first sentence, p. 55
issues.printed: The remark assumes oddness of ρ̄ at a real place of F and associates complex conjugation c ∈ G_F to that place, up to conjugacy. For every v with ρ̄(Frob_v) conjugate to ρ̄(c), it claims v is a level raising prime in its terminology and satisfies q_v ≡ −1 (mod ℓ).
issues.correction: “… then any v ∤ ℓ at which ρ̄ is unramified, with ρ̄(Frob_v) conjugate to ρ̄(c) and q_v ≡ −1 (mod ℓ) (for instance any v with Frob_v conjugate to c in Gal(F(ρ̄, ζ_ℓ)/F)), is a level raising prime.” When det ρ̄ = ε̄_ℓ (Case (PGL2)) the congruence follows from ρ̄(Frob_v) ~ ρ̄(c).
issues.reason: ρ̄(c) has eigenvalues 1, −1, so v is level raising iff q_v ≡ −1 (mod ℓ); ρ̄(Frob_v) ~ ρ̄(c) gives det ρ̄(Frob_v) = −1, which equals q_v mod ℓ only if det ρ̄ = ε̄_ℓ. Counterexample in Case (Wt1): the weight-one form of level 23 (projective image S_3, det = (−23/·)), ℓ = 5, v = 11: 11 is inert in Q(√−23), so ρ̄(Frob_11) ~ ρ̄(c), but 11 ≡ 1 (mod 5), so 11 is not a level raising prime. The remark is used in no proof.

issues.locator: Remark 12.2, second paragraph, second sentence, p. 55
issues.printed: The remark assumes that ρ̄ has projective image PSL_2(k), with |k| ≥ 5 and [F(ζ_ℓ) : F] > 2. It claims the existence of places v where the eigenvalue ratio of ρ̄(Frob_v) is q_v, with q_v ≢ ±1 (mod ℓ), and calls these level raising primes.
issues.correction: Add the hypothesis that some a ∈ F_ℓ^× ∖ {±1} is a square in k (e.g. ℓ ≥ 7, or [k : F_ℓ] even). Then choose λ ∈ k with λ² = a and use Chebotarev in the compositum of F(proj ρ̄) and F(ζ_ℓ), which are linearly disjoint because PSL_2(k) is simple.
issues.reason: An element of GL_2 with class in PSL_2(k) is z·h with h ∈ SL_2(k), so its eigenvalue ratio is μ² for an eigenvalue μ of h; if μ ∉ k then μ^{|k|} = μ^{−1} and a ratio in F_ℓ is ±1. So a ratio in F_ℓ ∖ {±1} must be a square in k. For ℓ = 5 and [k : F_5] odd, 2 and 3 are non-squares; e.g. F = Q with projective image PSL_2(F_5) ≅ A_5: q_v ≢ ±1 (mod 5) forces a ratio of order 4, but A_5 has no element of order 4. The hypothesis [F(ζ_5):F] = 4 > 2 holds. The remark is used in no proof.

issues.correction: For a general K the constant term of the characteristic polynomial is the diamond (central-character) operator ⟨v⟩, so det ρ_K = ψ times the nebentypus. At Taylor–Wiles level K^𝔇_{Σ,Q} (Q ≠ ∅) this is not ψ: the scalars Z_v^× (v ∈ Q) lie in K_0^𝔇(Q) and map onto Δ_v, so Δ_Q acts through the central character. Either define the Taylor–Wiles levels through ad^{−1} as in §13.4 (keeping d ≡ 1 mod t²), which makes ⟨d⟩_v the diamond operators of the O[Δ_Q]-structure and the determinant ψ; or keep the d-type level, state Theorem 14.5(ii) with x² − T_v x + ⟨v⟩, and in Theorem 14.6 twist ρ_{Σ,Q} by the square root of the ℓ-power-order character ψ·det(ρ_{Σ,Q})^{−1} (ℓ odd), as in Calegari–Geraghty [17, Thm 3.11], before mapping from R^𝔇_{Σ,Q} (whose lifts have determinant ψ).
issues.reason: Forms with a nontrivial Δ_v-character have central character ramified at v ∈ Q, and in weight one det ρ_π is the central character. Patching needs H_0(C^𝔇_{Σ,Q}) to be free over O[Δ_Q] (Proposition 14.1(2)), so such forms occur after localizing at m; but ψ is unramified outside S and ℓ, so the printed characteristic polynomial, and the existence of R^𝔇_{Σ,Q} ↠ T^𝔇_{Σ,Q} with determinant ψ, fail as printed. At level Q = ∅ with prime-to-ℓ nebentypus the two agree, so the minimal-level statements are unaffected once the Taylor–Wiles levels are corrected.

issues.locator: Theorem G, Introduction p. 7 (and footnote 1), and the sentence before Conjecture A, p. 60
issues.printed: On p. 7 the source cites [45, Theorem 1.3] for Conjecture A over CM fields with sufficiently large ℓ. Theorem G assumes ℓ > 20 and claims an integer µ ≥ 1 exists. Footnote 1 refers to [45, (1.2)] for the bound and says ℓ > 20 suffices for [F : Q] = 2. On p. 60 it cites [45, Theorem 1.1, Theorem 1.3] for part (ii) at sufficiently large ℓ.
issues.correction: [45, Theorem 1.3] gives ρ_m only modulo an ideal I with I^4 = 0, so it does not give Conjecture A(ii). The nilpotent-free result, whose bound is (1.2), is [45, Theorem 1.4 = Theorem 5.13]; it assumes ℓ unramified in F and a strictly regular weight (λ_{τ,1} > λ_{τ,2} for every τ), whereas the complexes C_K of §13 have trivial coefficients (λ = 0). So the cited results do not supply Conjecture A(ii) for C_K; Theorem G should also assume Conjecture A(ii) (and ℓ unramified in F), or cite a result covering trivial weight.
issues.reason: For n = 2 and F imaginary quadratic, the left side of [45, (1.2)] is 16 + 3(a_1 − a_2) + (b_1 − b_2) for λ_τ̃ = (a_1, a_2), λ_τ̃c = (b_1, b_2); its minimum over regular weights is 20, at λ = ((1,0),(1,0)), which is the footnote's ℓ > 20. At λ = 0 the Lan–Suh vanishing behind [45, Thm 5.10] fails already in degree 0. Also ℓ = 23 with F = Q(√−23) meets ℓ > 20 but is ramified in F. Theorem G as stated therefore rests on an input the citation does not provide; its other inputs (Conjectures C, D via Theorem 13.12) need only ℓ > 3.

Pigeonhole the α_i by the class of η_i in O_K^*/(O_K^*)^d, which has at most d^{[K:ℚ]} = O_{[L:ℚ]}(1) classes. Within one class, η_i = η₀e_i^d with e_i ∈ O_K^*; replace α_i by α_i/e_i, which leaves the ideal unchanged. Then Nm_{L/K}(uα_r/α_s) = 1, so every t_i = log|Nm_{L/K}(uα_r/α_s)|_{w_i} vanishes, and the stated height bound follows. The loss is a factor O_{[L:ℚ]}(1) in N + 1, so (2.1) is unchanged.
issues.reason: The boxes control only PUL(α_i), i.e. the differences of coordinates within each block, because P drops the block sums t_i. Units u ∈ O* = ker(Nm_{L/K}) have t_i = 0, but an arbitrary generator α_i of ℘_i^{ℓa_i}℘̄_i^{−ℓb_i}℘₀^{−ℓa₀}℘̄₀^{ℓb₀} has t_i(α_i) = log|Nm_{L/K}(α_i)|_{w_i}, the logarithm of a unit of K, which need not be bounded. "Norm 1" in the absolute sense gives only Σ_i t_i = 0. The step Σ max(x_v, 0) = Σ_i t_i + O(1) needs each t_i = O(1) (for example t₁ = T, t₂ = −T gives Σ max ≈ T). So the claimed bound on H(uα_r/α_s) is not justified as written, though the repair costs only a constant depending on [L : ℚ].

issues.locator: Proof of Theorem 8.2.1, p.59
issues.printed: The source assumes L^♭ + ⟨x⟩ integral, chooses a basis (e′_1, …, e′_n) with val(e′_i) = a′_i, and sets L′^♭ = ⟨e′_1, …, e′_{n−1}⟩. For x′ = e′_n it claims Int_{L^♭,V}(x) = Int_{L′^♭,V}(x′) and ∂Den_{L^♭,V}(x) = ∂Den_{L′^♭,V}(x′).
issues.correction: Replace the two claimed equalities by the equality of differences: with φ = Int_{L^♭,V} − ∂Den_{L^♭,V} and φ′ = Int_{L′^♭,V} − ∂Den_{L′^♭,V}, Theorem 6.1.3 cancels the horizontal parts, so φ(x) = Int(L^♭ + ⟨x⟩) − ∂Den(L^♭ + ⟨x⟩) = Int(L′^♭ + ⟨x′⟩) − ∂Den(L′^♭ + ⟨x′⟩) = φ′(x′). The induction hypothesis φ′ = 0 then gives φ(x) = 0 for x ∉ M(L^♭), which is all the rest of the proof uses.
issues.reason: Only the full functions Int_{L^♭}(x) = Int(L^♭ + ⟨x⟩) and ∂Den_{L^♭}(x) depend on the lattice L^♭ + ⟨x⟩ alone. Their horizontal and vertical parts depend on the hyperplane L^♭_F. By Definition 6.1.2, ∂Den_{L^♭,H}(x) and ∂Den_{L′^♭,H}(x′) are sums over integral L″ ⊇ L^♭ + ⟨x⟩ = L′^♭ + ⟨x′⟩ with the different conditions t(L″ ∩ L^♭_F) ≤ 1 and t(L″ ∩ L′^♭_F) ≤ 1; geometrically, Z(L^♭)_H ≠ Z(L′^♭)_H. So the two stated equalities do not follow from what precedes them. The step is repaired in one line and the theorem stands.

issues.locator: Remark 4.11.5, p.30 (final version; also arXiv v1); used in the proof of Lemma 9.2.2 (i), p.64
issues.correction: A lift g̃ ∈ J(F) of g ∈ SO(V)(F) has spinor norm η(g̃) = sn(g) in F^×/(F^×)², so η(g̃) = 1 forces sn(g) = 1. What the argument needs is only val η(g̃) = 0, since g̃ carries RZ^{(ℓ)}_G to RZ^{(ℓ + val η(g̃))}_G (§4.5) and N = RZ^{(0)}_G; that is available exactly when some isometry carrying L′ to L has spinor norm of even valuation, which the remark does not establish.
issues.reason: There are isometric pairs for which every isometry has spinor norm of odd valuation. Take m even and ε = −1: for m even and U unimodular, ϵ(ϖU) = χ(U), so V^−_m ≅ ϖ·H^−_{m,F}. Write H^−_m = M ⊥ ⟨w⟩ with M self-dual of rank n = m − 1, and let L ⊆ V be M with the scaled form, so that all its fundamental invariants are 1 and val(w) = 1. An element of SO(V)(F) stabilizing L preserves L_F and the line L^⊥_F, hence is a product of an even number of reflections in vectors of L or of L^⊥_F (for p odd the orthogonal group of a unimodular lattice is generated by the reflections in its vectors of unit norm, O'Meara 92:4); each such reflection has spinor norm of valuation 1, so the stabilizer has spinor norms of even valuation. Since V is isotropic, sn : SO(V)(F) → F^×/(F^×)² is surjective; choosing h with val sn(h) odd and L′ = hL gives isometric lattices such that every g ∈ SO(V)(F) with gL′ = L has val sn(g) odd. Remark 4.11.5 is the invariance input for Lemma 9.2.2 (i) (the O(W)(F)-invariance of Int^⊥_{L^♭,V}), hence for Proposition 9.2.3 and Theorem 9.3.2. The conclusion is presumably true — Theorem 4.15.1 asserts it, and for m = 4, ε = −1 it follows from Terstiege's explicit formulas (Remark 4.15.2) — and an automorphism of RZ_G outside J(F) shifting the components would supply it; but no such argument is given here, and this extraction did not settle it.

issues.locator: §7.1 (Cohen–Lenstra–Martinet comparison), p. 34 (arXiv v2)
issues.printed: The source claims projectivity of N_p over Z_p[Γ] because that ring is hereditary. It also asserts N_p ⊗ Q_p ≅ (𝓕_n)^𝒞_p ⊗ Q_p, citing torsion-freeness and the finite-index inclusion of N_p in (𝓕_n)^𝒞_p ≅ (Z_p[Γ])^n.
issues.correction: (𝓕_n)^𝒞_p ≅ (Z_p[Γ]/(Σ_{g∈Γ} g))^n, the n-th power of the augmentation ideal.
issues.reason: For 𝒞 the abelian |Γ|′-Γ-groups, (𝓕_n)^𝒞 = 𝓕_n^ab, and Corollary 3.10 of the paper gives 𝓕_n^ab ≅ (Z[Γ]/(Σ_g g))^n with no Γ-invariants, whereas (Z_p[Γ])^n has invariants Z_p^n. The argument goes through unchanged: finite-index Γ-sublattices of a lattice over the hereditary order Z_p[Γ] are projective with the same rational span, hence isomorphic (Serre, Linear representations, §16, Theorem 34, Corollary 2).

issues.locator: Statement of Theorem 5.12, p. 30, against Theorem 5.15 (p. 31), Lemma 6.1 and Theorem 6.2 (pp. 31–32) and Theorems 7.4–7.5 (pp. 35–36) (arXiv v2)
issues.printed: Theorem 5.12 takes an integer u ≥ 0 and asserts countable additivity of µ_u on A, the algebra generated by U_{C,H}. Theorem 5.15 takes an integer u and gives µ_u(V_{C,H}) = … . Theorem 6.2 introduces a random Γ-group X_u distributed according to µ_u and states its assertion for any integer u.
issues.correction: State Theorem 5.12 for every integer u. Its proof applies Lemma 5.10 to f_n(H, ℓ) = µ_{u,n}(U_{𝒞_ℓ,H}), g_n(H) = |Sur_Γ(𝓕_n, H)|/(|Aut_Γ(H)||Y(H)|^{n+u}) and g(H) = |Aut_Γ(H)|^{−1}|Y(H)|^{−u}. The inequality g_n ≤ g holds for every u, because |Sur_Γ(𝓕_n, H)| ≤ |Y(H)|^n by Corollary 3.8. Corollary 5.9 only needs u > −n, which holds for large n. So nothing in the argument uses u ≥ 0.
issues.reason: For u < 0, Theorems 5.15, 6.2 and 7.4–7.5 evaluate µ_u on Borel sets V_{𝒞,H} and integrate against µ_u. That requires µ_u to extend to a Borel measure, which is proved (Theorem 5.12, with Carathéodory extension) only for u ≥ 0 as printed. The main Theorems 1.2 and 1.4 use u = 1 and are unaffected. With the hypothesis dropped the statements hold. For example, at u = −1 and Γ = Z/2 the formula gives measure 0 to every finite abelianization, consistent with the free rank-one abelianization of 𝓕_n/(n−1 relations).

issues.printed: The proof takes m ∈ M(𝔽̄_p) with m̂ := ad_M(m) in Z_{M^ad}(ad_M(U)). From #F | e and the construction of U[e], it infers φ_m(U[e]) = {1}, equivalently m ∈ Z_M(U[e]). It declares the lemma proved by choosing U′ = U[e] and c(N) = e^{k(N)}.
issues.correction: The argument proves the inclusion Z_{M^ad}(ad_M(U)) ⊆ Z_M(U[e])/Z(M). This is what the applications use, and it suffices there. In Lemma 5.11 the Tate hypothesis gives Z_M(V[e]) = Z(M), hence Z_{M^ad}(ad_M(V)) = 1 and so Z_{M^ad}(Û) = 1. Either restate Lemma 5.12 as this inclusion, or supply a separate argument for the equality on U′.
issues.reason: The lemma asserts Z_{M^ad}(ad_M(U′)) = Z_M(U′)/Z(M) for U′ = U[e]. That needs, for every m with ad_M(m) centralising ad_M(U[e]), that m centralises U[e]. The proof takes m centralising the image of the larger group U. Then φ_m is a homomorphism U → F killed by U[e]. For m only centralising ad_M(U[e]), φ_m is a homomorphism U[e] → F, and U[e] need not lie in its kernel, because homomorphisms of U[e] to F need not extend to U. The inclusion needed for the stated equality is therefore not established.

issues.locator: Lemma 5.3, Proposition 5.2, Theorems 5.7 and 5.8, pp.25–31
issues.printed: Proposition 5.2 takes m ∈ Z_{>0} with Z(m) ≠ ∅ and, for odd b, requires √(m/D) ∈ Z for fixed D as in Theorem 2.4. Lemma 5.3 uses the same restriction and invokes [BK03, Theorem 4.11, (4.73), (4.74)] because d_0 and k do not depend on m. Theorems 5.7 and 5.8 derive bounds from Proposition 5.2 for, respectively, every m represented by (L, Q) and every positive integer m.
issues.correction: For b odd and m/D not a square, add this to the proof of Lemma 5.3. In [BK03, Thm. 4.11(ii)] (r odd), the m-dependence through d_0 = d_0(m) enters as log|4m/D_0²| − 2L′(χ_{D_0}, 3/2 − κ)/L(χ_{D_0}, 3/2 − κ). By the functional equation of L(s, χ_{D_0}), this is log m + 2L′(χ_{D_0}, κ − 1/2)/L(χ_{D_0}, κ − 1/2) + O(1): the log|D_0| terms cancel. The logarithmic derivative at κ − 1/2 ≥ 2 is bounded by |ζ′/ζ(2)|, and the χ_{d_0}-factors of σ_m(s) are bounded uniformly as in the proof of Proposition 5.2. So Lemma 5.3 (with O(1) uniform in m) and Proposition 5.2 hold for every m with Z(m) ≠ ∅. That is what Theorems 5.7–5.8 assert, and what Proposition 6.4 and Lemma 7.6 use.
issues.reason:
Theorem 5.8 is proved from equation (3.1), Proposition 3.2 and Proposition 5.2, so for b odd its proof covers only m ∈ D·(Q^×)². It is then applied to arbitrary integers:
- in Proposition 6.4 to M = Q(λ) for a difference λ of two lattice vectors ("Theorem 5.8(i) implies X^{b/2} ≪ −log|Q(λ_x)| ≪ A(M) ≪ M^{b/2} log M");
- in Lemma 7.6 to m = a_1(n)², a square but not in general D times a square.
Both feed Theorem 6.1 and Theorem 7.1, hence the main theorem for every odd b ≥ 3. For b even, d = (−1)^{r/2}det(L) does not depend on m and there is no gap. BK03 Theorem 4.11 was read in arXiv:math/0204100v2 (p.27): its r-odd formula contains log|4m/D_0²| and −2L′(χ_{D_0}, 3/2 − κ)/L(χ_{D_0}, 3/2 − κ).

issues.locator: §7.3, construction of μ, p.43
issues.printed: Given a_n ≠ 0, the source sets a_i = 0 throughout n + 1 ≤ i ≤ e^{e^{p^n}} and assigns a_i = 1 at i = ⌈e^{e^{p^n}}⌉. It claims Σ_{i≤n} a_ip^i ≡ μ mod p^N with N ≥ e^{e^{p^n}}, giving an integer x_n of size O(p^n) approximating μ mod p^N with N double-exponential in its size. It further claims the resulting lattice Λ has property 2.
issues.correction: Make the gaps double-exponential in the discriminant rather than in x_n: after a_n ≠ 0, set a_i = 0 for n < i < exp(exp(C·p^{2c(n+1)})) with C depending only on L (so that exp(C·p^{2c(n+1)}) exceeds the discriminant of L_n below). Then property (2) of Lemma 7.11 holds with L_n = span_Z{e_j + x_nf_j}, and the example stands.
issues.reason: Property (2) of Lemma 7.11 needs N_i ≥ e^{e^{D_i}}, where D_i is the discriminant of the approximating sublattice L_i. Here L_i = span_Z{e_j + x_nf_j : 1 ≤ j ≤ c}, with e_j, f_j orthogonal and Q positive definite. So D_i ≍ Π_j (Q(e_j) + x_n²Q(f_j)) ≥ x_n^{2c} ≥ p^{2cn}, because a_n ≠ 0 forces x_n ≥ p^n. The printed choice gives only N ≈ e^{e^{p^n}}, which is far below e^{e^{D_i}}, so the proof of Lemma 7.11 (m_i < e^{D_i} and (Y_Λ.Z(m_i)) > N_i ≥ e^{e^{D_i}} > e^{m_i}) does not apply. "Double-exponential in the size of x_n" is not double-exponential in D_i ≍ x_n^{2c}. The example is illustrative and not used for the main results.

These four are orthogonal and satisfy U^2 v = -v, so they span the (-1)-eigenspace of U^2 and give SL_2^4. The deleted proof in the source file makes the same statement: 'x_1, x_3, y_1, y_3 are orthogonal and generate the (-1)-eigenspace of U^2'.

The definition and the proof of Theorem 3.13 only use homomorphisms to F and its lift F̃_c, whose orders are prime to p. These factor through the prime-to-p quotient, so nothing changes. issues.locator: Proposition 14, pp.725–727, and Remark 16, p.727, in the published version, Annals of Mathematics 184 (2016), 709–744 (publisher PDF, SHA-256 814976ee…f40a); also footnote 4, p.712
issues.printed: Proposition 14 claims that nearby CM points of one type, sharing a projection to X(1)×X(1), belong to a Hecke curve of low degree, for both Heegner and anti-Heegner points. Remark 16 says that anti-Heegner CM points lie on no Hecke curves and consequently repel. Footnote 4 says Proposition 14’s stronger repulsion assertion resolves the 2-to-1 ambiguity in [BT13].
issues.correction: Proposition 14 holds for Heegner CM points (CM⁺) only, with Lemma 15 applied with h₀ = 1 (erratum Proposition 2.1). Close anti-Heegner CM points lie on low-degree conjugate Hecke curves instead. The first clause of Remark 16 (Hecke curves contain no anti-Heegner points) is true; its repulsion claim is false.
issues.reason: The real-analytic involution conjugating the second factor preserves the hyperbolic metric and swaps Heegner and anti-Heegner CM points, so anti-Heegner points cannot all repel. In general no h₀ ∈ SL₂(Z) reduces to the non-identity coset of the stabilizer H in its normalizer, which is where the proof fails (erratum §§1–2). The appeal in footnote 4 therefore rests on the withdrawn part; the main theorems hold by the corrected argument of the erratum.

issues.correction: ξ((h¹/z)_Q) = ξ(h²_Q)·∏_{𝔩|f, 𝔩∤p} ξ(Z_p[[G_{p∞f}/D_𝔩]]_Q), D_𝔩 the decomposition group of 𝔩; equivalently ξ((h¹/z)_Q) = ξ(H²_Q) with H² = lim_{K'} H²(O_{K'}[1/pf], Z_p(1)), which is the module of Johnson-Leung–Kings §7.2. issues.reason: z is generated by the elliptic units of the single modulus p^n f (Kato §15.5), whose projection to a character χ carries ∏_{𝔩|f,𝔩∤p}(1 − χ(𝔩)Frob_𝔩^{−1}) (Johnson-Leung–Kings Lemma 7.7); JLK accordingly pair it with H² over O_K[1/pf]. BT's h² is the class-group limit, which Kato (15.6.2) identifies at height one with H² over O_K[1/p]. By purity, 0 → H²(O[1/p]) → H²(O[1/pf]) → ⊕_{𝔩|f,𝔩∤p} Z_p[[G/D_𝔩]] → 0, and since D_𝔩 has Z_p-rank one each term is torsion but not pseudo-null. On the trivial-character component 1 − Frob_𝔩^{−1} is a non-unit even after inverting p, so the printed equality fails whenever f has a prime factor not above p, and footnote 3's "identical" is false for h². The same imprecision is in Kato's quotation of Rubin (Astérisque 295, Theorem 15.2(2)); Rubin's elliptic units include all moduli g|f.

issues.printed: Lemma 3.15 asserts, using the preceding notation, Σ_{x∈D(k)} Σ_{j=1}^{r} #{y ∈ C̃_j(k^alg) : ν_j(y) = x} ≤ (q + 1)r + 2q^{1/2} · Σ_{j=1}^{r} g_g(C_j).
issues.correction: The count of geometric branches over k-points needs an extra term for the non-rational branches through rational singular points. For a geometrically integral curve C with normalization of genus g and arithmetic genus p_a, one has Σ_{x∈C(k)} #ν^{−1}(x) ≤ #C̃(k) + 2 Σ_x δ_x ≤ q + 1 + 2g q^{1/2} + 2(p_a − g). The constant q + 4q^{1/2} + 3 in Theorem 9.1 and in Theorems 1.5, 1.7, 10.1 and Corollaries 1.11, 1.14, 1.15, obtained from Lemma 3.15 in (9.8), is not established by the v2 argument.
issues.reason: Counterexample. Let D ⊂ P² over k = F_3 be the projective closure of y² = x²(x − 1). It is geometrically integral (r = 1) with normalization P¹, parametrized by x = t² + 1, y = t(t² + 1), so g_g = 0 and the right side is q + 1 = 4. D(F_3) consists of (0,0), (1,0), (2,1), (2,2) and the point at infinity. The origin is an ordinary node with tangent cone y² + x² = 0. Since −1 is not a square in F_3, its two branches t = ±i are defined only over F_9. The left side is therefore 2 + 4 = 6 > 4. The proof's flaw: Lemma 3.17 correctly relates the product of Z*_{D,k}(ζT) over ζ ∈ μ_d to the zeta functions of the C̃_j over k′. But the zeros and poles of Z*_{D,k} cannot be read off from that product. Here Z*_{D,k}(T) = (1 + T)/((1 − T)²(1 − qT)), and the extra factor (1 + T)/(1 − T) disappears under T ↦ −T. The bound with q + 1 + 2g q^{1/2} + 2(p_a − g) follows from Weil's bound for C̃ together with b_x ≤ δ_x + 1 ≤ 2δ_x at singular points, and it is attained in the example. The general reducible, weighted sum in (9.8) needs the analogous count, including intersections of Frobenius-conjugate components. Noted by the extraction (gap G1, items bad-branch-bound and global-sum-source), which checked the page image.

issues.correction: There are only finitely many k-isomorphism classes of nonsuperspecial K3 surfaces X over k admitting a polarization H of such a degree 2md with (i)–(iii). The polarized pairs themselves need not be finite in number.
issues.reason: On a fixed eligible (X, H) of degree 2m_0 d, the line bundles H^{⊗ℓ^j} have degree 2(ℓ^{2j} m_0)d. Then m = ℓ^{2j} m_0 satisfies (i) and (ii), and (iii) is unchanged. This gives infinitely many pairwise non-isomorphic polarized pairs on one surface; the paper does not require polarizations to be primitive. The proof bounds NS(X_k̄) and then the surfaces. issues.reason: Take a odd with a² + 4 squarefree, for example a = 13 or 101 (D = 173 or 10205 = 5·13·157). Then D = a² + 4 ≡ 5 (mod 8) is a fundamental discriminant, and a² + 4 is squarefree for a positive proportion of a. For the principal class, (a + √D)/2 has regular continued fraction [a; a, a, …]. A regular partial quotient a in an odd position becomes a run of a − 1 twos in the minus continued fraction, so the reduced period is ((a + 2, 2, …, 2)) with a − 1 twos, and ℓ_A = a. Meanwhile ε_D = ((a + √D)/2)² = (a² + 2 + a√D)/2, so log ε_D ≈ 2 log a, and ℓ_A / log ε_D → ∞. A direct computation for a = 5, 7, 13, 21, 51, 101, 201, 401 gives ℓ_A = a. In each case the product of the reduced w over the period equals ε_D, as in (6.3), which confirms that ℓ_A is the paper's quantity. The remark is not used elsewhere in the paper.

issues.printed: Corollary 1.1.15 takes any connected reductive G over Q_p, a Q_p-rational Levi M, a minuscule μ: G_m → M, and [b_M] ∈ B(M)_b with ([b_M], {μ}) G-admissible. It claims some w ∈ W(G, M) := N_G(M)/M makes ([b_M], {w·μ}) M-admissible. The proof invokes (1.1.13) for w* ∈ W(G*, M*) making ([b_{M*}], {w*·μ*}) M*-admissible.
issues.correction: Replace N_G(M)/M by the absolute Weyl group W(G, T) of a maximal torus T ⊂ M with μ ∈ X_*(T), as in Proposition 1.1.13. Equivalently: some G(Q̄_p)-conjugate μ′ of μ factoring through T makes ([b_M], {μ′}) M-admissible.
issues.reason: The printed statement fails already for split G. Take G = GL_3, M = GL_1 × GL_2 (blocks of sizes 1 and 2), μ = (0,1,0) and b_M = diag(p,1,1), which is basic in M. Then ([b_M], {μ}) is G-admissible: its Newton point (1,0,0) equals the dominant μ̄, and both have κ_G = 1. But κ_M(b_M) = (1,0), while κ_M(μ) = (0,1). Since the blocks have different sizes, N_G(M) = M, so W(G, M) is trivial and no w in it helps. The permutation of the first two coordinates, in W(G, T) = S_3, does. The proof transports to the quasi-split inner form and applies Proposition 1.1.13. That proposition gives w* in the absolute Weyl group W(G*, T*), not in N_{G*}(M*)/M*, so the proof establishes the corrected statement. The only use is in the proof of Corollary 1.1.17, p.13, for G not necessarily quasi-split. It cites "Lemma 1.1.13" (the quasi-split Proposition 1.1.13) in the form w ∈ W(G, T). The corrected Corollary 1.1.15 is exactly what that step needs, so the later results stand. Checked on the page images. Noted by the extraction (source discrepancy 2, items N29 and N32), which also verified the Weyl-group computation by machine.

issues.locator: Proof of Lemma 2.2.8, p.28, in the author PDF https://math.berkeley.edu/~swshin/HT.pdf (41 pp., created 27 January 2021, SHA-256 fd22990b…52db), the latest version found; the published text, Duke Math. J. 171 (2022), 1559–1614, was not collated
issues.printed: The source sets G′ = G × T, V′ = V ⊕ V and X′ = X × {h_T}, claiming (G′, X′) ↪ (G_{V′}, H_{V′}). Restriction of I_{s′_0} to A_T is said to give I_{s′_0} → T, hence I_{s′_0} → T → G^ab. It invokes Corollary 2.1.9 for surjectivity of I_{s′_0} → I_{s_0} and deduces that I_{s′_0} → G^ab factors through I_{s_0}, citing this factorization over Q_ℓ for every ℓ ≠ p.
issues.correction: Take G′ = G ×_{G^ab} T, the pairs (g, t) with the same image in G^ab. This lies in GSp(V ⊕ V, ψ ⊕ ψ), and X′ = X × {h_T} still maps into it because h^ab is constant on X. The kernel of G′ → G is T ∩ G^der, which dies in G^ab, so the composite I_{s′_0} → T → G^ab does factor through I_{s_0}. The rest of the proof then goes through.
issues.reason: Read literally, the construction fails at two points. First, G × T acting on V ⊕ V does not preserve ψ ⊕ ψ up to a scalar when the similitude factors of g and t differ, so it is not a subgroup of G_{V′}. Second, the claimed factorization fails. The CM automorphisms (1, t), t ∈ T, act trivially on A_{s_0} and by t on A_T, and they preserve the tensors cutting out G × T. So 1 × T lies in I_{s′_0}, and also in the kernel of I_{s′_0} → I_{s_0}. But under I_{s′_0} → T → G^ab it maps onto G^ab, as T is a maximal torus of G. So the map does not factor through I_{s_0} unless G^ab = 1. The same happens over Q_ℓ, so the justification "as this is true over Q_ℓ" fails too. Surjectivity of I_{s′_0} → I_{s_0} alone cannot give a factorization. What is needed is that the kernel maps trivially, and the fibre product above provides this. Lemma 2.2.8 is used in the proof of Proposition 2.2.2 (p.28). Noted by the extraction (source discrepancy 7, item T23) as a descent gate; the analysis and the fibre-product repair are given here.

issues.correction: Assume in addition that S is reduced and separated (for example a variety). Then two automorphisms that agree on a dense set of points agree, because their equalizer is a closed subscheme containing a dense set, and the proof applies.
issues.reason: The proof ends "Γ_{w_0} is dense in S … and it follows that σ = w_0". That step fails without reducedness or separatedness. For the affine line with doubled origin, the automorphism exchanging the two origins fixes the dense set of other k-points; again W is trivial. The lemma is applied on p.30 to a maximal torus T, which is reduced and separated, so nothing changes. Checked on the page image. Noted by the extraction (source discrepancy 4, item G16); the separatedness counterexample is added here.

issues.printed: The source partitions X_{d,d} into X^i_{d,d} according to the least i with Stab φ_i = Stab φ_{i+1}, for pairs (φ, ψ), taking φ_i to mean truncation through order i. It justifies the partition by asserting that Stab φ_i ≠ Stab φ_{i+1} forces the dimension of Stab φ_{i+1} to be smaller by at least 1.
issues.correction: A strict inclusion Stab φ_{i+1} ⊊ Stab φ_i of algebraic subgroups need not lower the dimension. issues.reason: A proper closed subgroup of the same dimension is a union of fewer connected components of the same identity component. issues.locator: Theorem 11.3 and its proof, p.971, in the published version, Annals of Mathematics 189 (2019), 945–978 (public copy of the published PDF at bimsa.net, SHA-256 1eab0797…a0ab)
issues.printed: Theorem 11.3 takes a positive integer k, r ≥ 2, m as above, and (w, u, v) : Δ^k → Ω̂ × X × J^n_r X. If its image lies in V_{k,m} × V_{n,r}, Tv has image in W_{n,r}, and v restricts to u, it asserts existence of g ∈ G(C) with (w, u, v) = L(w, g, r). The proof writes g(t) = gn(t) with n(t) ∈ N and claims that the restriction of v to u forces n(t) to be identically the identity.
issues.correction: "v restricts to u" is not defined, and read as the zeroth-order condition used in the proof, namely that the value of v is u, the theorem is false. A first-order compatibility must be added: du equals the first-order part of v applied to dw, as holds for every L(w, g, r), or the full chain-rule compatibility of the jet v along w with the jets of u. The proof's last step must use it.
issues.reason:
Work locally on a modular curve (n = k = 1) with Γ torsion-free, near a point where q′ ≠ 0. Put w(t) = 2t, u(t) = q(t) and v(t) = J_r q(id_r(t)). Then:
- The m-jets of u are those of q ∘ (z ↦ z/2) ∘ w, so they lie in V_{k,m}.
- v lies in V_{n,r}, and Tv lies in W_{n,r}, since v moves along the leaf through the identity.
- The value of v at t is q(t) = u(t).
By Theorem 11.2, any g with u = q ∘ g ∘ w is z ↦ γ(z/2) with γ ∈ Γ. For such g, J_r(q ∘ g) at w(t) = 2t has first derivative q′(t)/2, while v has q′(t), so (w, u, v) ≠ L(w, g, r) for every g. In the proof, the leaf decomposition of v gives g(t) = τ_{−t}, the translation, with trivial leaf constant and n(t) = τ_{−t} ≠ id, although the zeroth-order condition holds. Every L(w, g, r) satisfies du = v_1 dw, which fails here (q′ ≠ 2q′). The same wording is in arXiv v3. The Ax–Schanuel theorems themselves are not claimed to fail. Noted by the extraction (item triple-characterization-obligation), which gave this example.

So no φ with z ∘ φ = id need exist, and rank(z) can be smaller than dim U. Full rank of the formal matrix r is what makes the linear recovery work. issues.printed: Theorem 4.19 takes K to be a number field or a one-variable function field, S quasi-projective over K, π : X → S a smooth relative curve with maximal variation and genus g > 1, and α a line bundle of positive degree on the fibers of X. It asserts the relative Bogomolov conjecture for i_α^m : X^m_{/S} → J^m_{/S} whenever m ≥ dim S + 1. In §1.6, maximal variation requires the moduli morphism S → M_{g,R} to be generically finite.
issues.correction: For a function field K of a curve over k, the hypothesis must be maximal variation of a model over k (equivalently, as the proof says, bigness of the relevant adelic line bundles over k rather than over K), which excludes isotrivial families. With that hypothesis, or for K a number field, the statement stands.
issues.reason: Counterexample to the function-field case: k algebraically closed of characteristic 0, K = k(t), S = Spec K, X = C₀ ×_k K for a smooth projective curve C₀/k of genus > 1, and α of degree 1. The moduli morphism Spec K → M_{g,K} is a point, hence generically finite, so X → S has maximal variation in the sense of §1.6. But every point of C₀(k) has canonical height 0 in the constant Jacobian, and these points are Zariski dense in X, so part (1) fails for m = 1 = dim S + 1; constant products give the same failure for the other parts. The proof itself notes that "we need the bigness of the adelic line bundles over k instead of over K", which a constant family does not have. The main uniform Bogomolov theorem excludes isotrivial families and is unaffected. Found by the extraction (items 185–189, 262–266).
